item_title: Brent and WTI both extended Sunday evening's decline into Monday's US session, with both benchmarks' futures below $100 a barrel and US crude (November WTI) down nearly 4% at $92.28 by mid-morning ET.
mechanism: Two forces that had been pulling oil in opposite directions this month converged onto the same side for the first time in this month's record: a genuine supply-side data point (JPMorgan's satellite-tracked 2.9 million bpd of Saudi crude now moving through Hormuz, up from 700,000 bpd in August, reported 09-20) and a demand/risk-premium signal (hopes of US-Iran diplomatic contact around this week's UN General Assembly). Either alone has moved this thread's price before without holding; together, on the same day, they explain a decline that continued rather than round-tripping the way this month's escalation headlines usually do.

scenarios.direction: The decline holds into Monday's settle and extends toward the low-$90s/high-$90s range for WTI if the UNGA week produces even a symbolic US-Iran diplomatic contact, with the Hormuz reroute data giving traders a fundamentals-based floor under the de-escalation story rather than a headline-only one.
scenarios.why: This month's record shows escalation headlines repeatedly failing to hold a price move this month once a session's data catches up (the 09-18 entry: fresh Saudi-Houthi clashes revived the premium intraday, then prices resumed their decline into the close) — a genuine supply data point is a stronger floor for a move than sentiment alone has been.
scenarios.precedent: The 09-17 move is the direct precedent: Aramco's concrete pipeline-restart plan (not just a claim) was what actually moved Brent down toward $102 intraday, while unconfirmed attack claims earlier in the month moved price only briefly.

scenarios.direction: The move reverses by Monday's close or Tuesday's session if the US-Iran diplomatic signal turns out to be as thin as Trump merely "considering" a Pezeshkian meeting, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard's same-day warning about new weapons is read as the more durable signal — the same headline-reversal pattern seen repeatedly this month.
scenarios.why: A single mid-session diplomatic hope is a thinner basis for a multi-day trend than a verified supply number; this month's record shows Brent giving back a "diplomacy" or "de-escalation" move within a session more than once when the underlying military situation did not actually change.
scenarios.precedent: The 09-18 session recorded exactly this shape of reversal (a midday round-trip to flat that did not hold into the close, in the other direction) — a precedent for how quickly this market has reversed a same-day read this month, not a hypothetical caution.

context_note: Reads directly against Red Sea Shock's own running question — whether the Yanbu claim's "attempted and thwarted" framing (09-20 finalize) is corroborated by actual barrels moving rather than just dueling statements. The Hormuz flow data is the first hard number on that question; Monday's price move is the market's own answer, provisional until it survives a full session.

item_title: Apollo chief economist Torsten Sløk warned Monday that the credit propping up hundreds of billions of dollars in AI data-center investment rests on one assumption Wall Street hasn't stress-tested: hyperscalers growing combined operating cash flow from $600 billion in 2025 to $2 trillion by 2030.
mechanism: The credit financing the AI buildout — GPU-collateralized loans, data-center asset-backed securities, Nvidia's own vendor-financing guarantees — is underwritten against a specific forward assumption rather than against cash flow that exists today: that the hyperscalers (Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and peers) roughly triple their collective operating cash flow, from $600bn in 2025 to $2tn by 2030, to cover the capex those loans are funding. Sløk's point is that this is a single assumption carrying the whole structure — if the cash flow growth comes in short, the mechanism runs in reverse: lenders reprice the risk (credit spreads widen), borrowers respond by cutting the capex those spreads were funding, and the slowdown is large enough to register in US GDP growth. It is the debt-market mirror of the same over-valuation question ESMA raised from the equity side the same Monday.

scenarios.direction: The assumption holds closely enough to keep credit priced roughly where it is through 2026-2027 — hyperscaler cash flow grows on a path consistent with the $2tn 2030 target, the buildout's investment-grade-rated financing (as distinct from the junk-rated, GPU-collateralized layer beneath it) keeps clearing, and capex plans are not cut.
scenarios.why: The hyperscalers funding most of the buildout's capex (Google's TPU buildout, Meta's Hyperion, Amazon's own compute spend) still generate the bulk of their cash flow from established, profitable core businesses (search, cloud, retail) rather than from the AI trade itself, giving them room to absorb a slower AI-revenue ramp without the credit structure underneath needing to reprice.
scenarios.precedent: Through 2026, BlackRock's GIP, KKR and sovereign-wealth co-investors continuing to buy INTO hyperscaler-adjacent infrastructure (the $40bn Aligned deal, the $10bn Helix venture) rather than pulling back — real capital still underwriting the buildout on the assumption Sløk describes, not yet a market that has repriced it.

scenarios.direction: The assumption breaks first at the structure's weakest, most levered layer — a CoreWeave- or Oracle-shaped credit event, not a hyperscaler-wide one — before spreading into the wider financing stack Sløk is describing, with capex cuts following the credit event rather than preceding it.
scenarios.why: The credit market has already shown an early version of exactly this mechanism: CoreWeave financed at 9.75% GPU-collateralized just as Nvidia's CDS widened (07-27) and Moody's named CoreWeave and Oracle together "AI's weakest credit link" (07-25) — a real credit-market reaction to leverage concerns that predates today's note and shows the mechanism can activate at the leveraged edge of the buildout before touching the hyperscalers' own investment- grade paper.
scenarios.precedent: The 07-25 Moody's call and the 07-27 Nvidia CDS widening are a directly on-point precedent — a real, dated instance of credit spreads moving on AI-buildout leverage concerns, not a hypothetical.

context_note: Landed the same Monday as ESMA's formal warning (above) that stretched AI valuations risk an "abrupt" correction — read together, one is the equity-market statement of the risk and this is the credit-market statement of the same underlying question: whether the cash flow the buildout is being financed against actually arrives on schedule.

item_title: Chinese customs data released over the weekend showed rare-earth magnet shipments to the US fell to 512 tonnes in August — down 20% from July and 13% below August 2025 — the fastest pace of decline since the pandemic on Capital Economics' read, days before Trump hosts Xi.
mechanism: The same Sunday meeting produced two moves in opposite directions because they serve different purposes for Beijing: a costless cooperative gesture (proposing an AI notification "dialogue," which commits China to nothing concrete and can be walked back) alongside continued tightening on the one lever — rare-earth magnet licensing — that gives Beijing real leverage heading into Thursday's summit. The customs data (August shipments, released before the meeting) is not itself a response to Sunday's talks, but the pattern it confirms — Beijing "willing to test the limits of the truce," per Capital Economics — is the backdrop Bessent's own "has not been up to par" framing was responding to going in.

scenarios.direction: Rare-earth shipment volumes recover toward the truce-era baseline in September/October data as a goodwill gesture ahead of or following the Trump-Xi summit, alongside progress on the AI Dialogue mechanism — the two threads converging rather than diverging once the summit itself is behind both sides.
scenarios.why: Both governments have a shared interest in the 11-10 tariff truce holding, and rare-earth licensing is the more easily reversible of Beijing's two levers (unlike a structural export-control regime change) if the summit produces a genuine reset.
scenarios.precedent: The record after the Busan truce shows export volumes broadly recovering from a May 2025 low of 46.4 tonnes once the initial truce took hold — Beijing has already demonstrated it will use the licensing spigot in both directions, not just tighten it.

scenarios.direction: The decline continues through Q4 regardless of the summit outcome, with the AI Dialogue proposal remaining a talk-track with no enforcement mechanism while rare-earth licensing stays the actual point of leverage — the summit producing atmosphere, not a change in the underlying trend this data shows.
scenarios.why: Some Chinese suppliers are reported (Reuters, via the same source) to be independently declining US shipments out of fear of Beijing's own sanctions on a US supply-chain monitor, a firm-level chilling effect that a government-to-government dialogue on AI does not address and would not reverse quickly even if licensing eased.

context_note: Sits alongside The Cross-Border Rate Leg' and CHIPS Equity Pivot's own record of the Sunday meeting — this entry is about the one concrete, adversarial data point inside an otherwise cooperative-sounding readout, not a restatement of the meeting itself.

item_title: SoftBank's roughly $11bn bond sale to fund its next OpenAI payment drew more than $20bn of early orders on Tuesday, with initial pricing talk of 8.75% to 9.875% — the highest yields SoftBank has ever offered on dollar bonds.
mechanism: SoftBank has to hand OpenAI $10bn on 10-01 and is raising it in the junk-bond market at BB+ (S&P and Fitch), so the guidance of 8.75% to 9.875% is the marginal price of funding an AI-equity commitment with unsecured debt when the 10-year Treasury sits near 5%. Books above $20bn on a $10bn dollar deal say the window is open; the record coupons say the price of keeping it open is rising, as with its 2031 notes moving from 6.7% in January to 8.2% in early September.

scenarios.direction: The deal prices on 09-24 at or inside the initial talk on an oversubscribed book and settles 09-29, confirming that access holds at a higher price and keeping the 10-01 OpenAI payment funded from the bond market rather than asset sales.
scenarios.why: Every SoftBank financing lever this month cleared on demand above target: the Arm-backed margin loan drew ~$7bn of offers against a $3-5bn goal and was upsized from $20bn to $25bn on 09-18, and the bridge loan was fully repaid on 09-15.
scenarios.precedent: Son All-In 09-18 entry: the Arm margin loan was upsized to $25bn on oversubscribed demand at SOFR+225bp, the same week the dollar-bond timetable slipped without harm.

scenarios.direction: The bonds price wide of talk or trade poorly in the after-market, repeating the pattern of AI-linked junk paper that clears at issue and then reprices in secondary, and pushing the cost of the next SoftBank raise higher.
scenarios.why: A 9.875% seven-year coupon leaves little room; the Jane Street / Oklahoma data-center green bond issued at ~8.9% in August already trades at 11.3%, and Reuters reports AI issuers being forced to pay concessions to complete deals.
scenarios.precedent: The Jane Street 149MW Oklahoma lease-backed junk bond (issued August, ~8.9%, now 11.3% in secondary), logged on AI Debt Gets Rated.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime reading (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 Fed hike and the 10-year's move to about 5%; it is read here for its long-end-pressure logic only, not updated.

item_title: Investors are pricing AI-related investment-grade bonds wider than the rest of the market: spreads on AI issuers sit near 115 basis points against 78 for broad investment-grade, Reuters reported Tuesday, with Goldman Sachs projecting a record $420bn of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, up 60%.
mechanism: Supply, not default risk: hyperscalers and their data-center vehicles are expected to issue a record $420bn next year, and investors who fear being over-concentrated in the same names demand a new-issue premium, so AI issuers pay roughly 115bp against 78bp for the broad index. Buyers are also aggregating parent-guaranteed vehicles back to the tech parent, which shrinks how much any one buyer will hold and turns each large deal into a test of the marginal bid.

scenarios.direction: The premium widens further as the 2027 supply arrives, and the first deal that fails to clear at a workable concession forces capex plans or financing structures to change.
scenarios.why: Reuters reports some hyperscaler deals already drawing thinner demand than marquee issuers are used to and trading poorly after pricing, with investors deliberately holding cash to buy later at wider spreads.
scenarios.precedent: Alphabet's August sale needed a large concession (BNY research note cited by Reuters) and the Jane Street Oklahoma bond has repriced from ~8.9% to 11.3% in secondary.

scenarios.direction: The premium stays contained because the borrowers are cash-rich and outside-AI buyers keep bidding, so the split is a pricing nuisance rather than a rationing of credit.
scenarios.why: Portfolio managers quoted by Reuters say they do not fear default, and heavily oversubscribed AI-linked paper such as Meta's $2.3bn CleanSpark-lease junk deal (~$10bn of demand) shows buyers exist at the right yield.
scenarios.precedent: Meta's 09-21 junk-rated lease deal drew about $10bn of orders for $2.3bn at 8.25%, on Circular Financing.

context_note: This reads Reuters' 09-22 survey of portfolio managers, not a market-wide spread series; the 115bp and 78bp figures are Goldman and ICE BofA readings cited there.

item_title: The 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 4bp to 4.951% Monday — down from last week's 19-year high of 5.041% — and the 30-year eased to 5.284%, tied explicitly by CNBC's own reporting to falling oil prices and a global easing of government borrowing costs, not to Treasury's own TGA-funded buyback campaign, which goes unmentioned.
mechanism: This snapshot's standing rate_regime reading (asof 08-25) already carries a Treasury-buyback-vs-external-driver tension on the long end — the 30-year sat near 5.20-5.24% off a mix of the Fed's hawkish hold, structural federal-borrowing-cost pressure (three 2026 30-year auctions clearing above 5%), and one direct Treasury intervention (the 08-19 buyback-size doubling that produced a partial reversal). Today's move is the same transmission mechanism running through a different channel: falling oil (itself moved by Iran's Hormuz- reopening offer, on Red Sea Shock) reads as easier global borrowing conditions and pulls the long end down alongside German bunds and UK gilts on the same session, with Treasury's own buyback calendar reported as inactive. Treasury's Long-End Defense's own record this month is now five-for-five: every large move has an external explanation (Fed policy, jobs data, oil) rather than the buyback campaign itself, in both directions — todays's move extends that pattern rather than breaking it.

scenarios.direction: The long end continues easing through the UN General Assembly week if Iran's Hormuz-reopening offer holds up under the in-person discussions reported for this week, extending oil's decline and compounding the "external driver, not the buyback" pattern into a sixth consecutive instance.
scenarios.why: Every external-driver move this thread has logged in September held through at least the following session rather than round-tripping intraday, unlike the standalone geopolitical- headline spikes on Red Sea Shock that have repeatedly failed to hold once a session's harder data caught up.
scenarios.precedent: The 08-19 JGB/Treasury sequence is the closest precedent for a cross-border rate move landing on the long end the same way — though that one included a genuine Treasury intervention (the buyback-size doubling) as a partial counter-move, which is explicitly absent from today's reporting.

scenarios.direction: The move reverses within the week if the Hormuz offer turns out to be a negotiating gambit rather than a real de-escalation step — the same "offer, not a signed deal" gap this map's own iran-hormuz-restricted-zone-boundaries ledger entry has been unable to close since 09-07.
scenarios.why: This map's standing rate_regime context already flags that September's hawkish-hold read has been repeatedly challenged by data that later proved partial or reversed (the July jobs report's hike-relief read, not a recession signal) — a Hormuz offer with no signed agreement behind it fits the same pattern of a headline that moves markets before its substance is confirmed.
scenarios.precedent: Red Sea Shock's own 09-18 entry: fresh Saudi-Houthi clashes revived the risk premium intraday, then prices resumed their decline into the close once the session's harder data caught up — evidence this market has round-tripped headline-only moves before.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime reading is five weeks stale (asof 08-25, pending its next /week-scale refresh) — this interpretation reads today's move against that snapshot's own logic (external-driver-not-buyback) rather than updating the standing reading itself, which is out of scope for a daily pass.

item_title: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said Monday the Fed will likely need to raise rates further, arguing that "earlier and incremental policy firming is better and less disruptive than later and larger" action, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, speaking in London, said he is watching whether AI data-center construction is "spilling out of its own lane" and pushing output beyond what the economy can absorb.
mechanism: Two Fed presidents are tying inflation to demand, not just oil, and one is naming AI data-center construction as a possible source of overheating. That links the buildout to the policy rate: if officials read capex as demand pressure, the reaction function that keeps the long end near 5% is tied to the same spending that the bond and equity markets are financing.

scenarios.direction: Hawkish talk plus strong data (Wednesday's flash PMIs, Thursday's claims) firms the case for an October hike and pushes the 10-year through last week's 5.04% high, tightening financing conditions for the AI-debt stack.
scenarios.why: Markets already price roughly even odds of a 10-28 hike, so any confirmation of demand-led inflation moves the odds and the long end together.
scenarios.precedent: The 09-16 hike: the 10-year cleared 5% the next day and bank stocks had their worst day since February (Treasury's Long-End Defense 09-17 entry).

scenarios.direction: Falling oil offsets the hawkish tone and the long end stays in a 4.9-5.0% range, with Fed rhetoric largely priced.
scenarios.why: The 10-year ended Tuesday unchanged at 4.96% despite both speeches, after five oil declines took Brent down about 12%.
scenarios.precedent: 09-21: the 10-year fell more than 4bp to 4.951% on falling oil while Musalem's Reuters interview was published the same day.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) still frames the Fed as holding at 3.50%-3.75%; the target range is now 3.75%-4.00%, so this reading is stale on the level and used here only for the reaction-function logic.

item_title: US business activity grew at its fastest pace in more than five years in September, S&P Global's flash PMI showed Wednesday: the composite output index rose to 58.4 from 56.0, services reached 58.7 and manufacturing 57.0, while input costs rose at the steepest rate in four years.
mechanism: A composite PMI at a five-year high with input costs at a four-year high and rising backlogs is the demand-led inflation story that Fed presidents Musalem, Goolsbee and Collins made in words this week. It raises the odds the Fed keeps hiking after 09-16, and higher expected policy rates lift the 10-year, which is why yields jumped 7bp on the release. The long end has mostly followed oil and the Fed rather than Treasury's own buyback in September, and this is the Fed leg.

scenarios.direction: The 10-year holds above 5% through Thursday's claims data and the 09-24 SoftBank pricing, with October hike odds rising from about 53%, tightening financing conditions for the AI-debt stack.
scenarios.why: Strong activity plus surging input costs is the data mix that has driven the long end higher before, and oil, which had been offsetting it, bounced back Wednesday morning.
scenarios.precedent: 09-16 to 09-18: after the Fed's hike the 10-year cleared 5% and closed at 5.01% on 09-18, its highest since 2007, tracking the Fed/oil axis (Treasury's Long-End Defense entries).

scenarios.direction: The PMI jump fades as a one-month survey reading, oil resumes its decline on US-Iran diplomacy and the 10-year settles back below 5%.
scenarios.why: Flash PMIs are revised and survey readings are noisy; the 10-year ended Tuesday at 4.96% despite two hawkish Fed speeches because oil fell for a fifth session.
scenarios.precedent: 09-17: an oil-driven rebound pulled the 10-year from above 5% to 4.93% at the close within a day of the post-hike selloff.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 hike and still describes a 3.50%-3.75% hold; it is used for the long-end logic only. All Wednesday levels are intraday reads.

item_title: The 10-year Treasury yield jumped more than 14 basis points Wednesday afternoon to 5.116% — its highest since July 2007 and its biggest one-day move in nearly 18 months — after a Treasury auction of 5-year notes drew weak demand and Fed Governor Michael Barr said "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to bring inflation to target.
mechanism: A weak 5-year note auction is a direct test of this thread's own question — whether Treasury can keep selling duration at yields the market finds attractive while the Fed is still hiking — and today it failed that test: the auction priced 5.033% against a 4.186% six-auction average, with indirect (largely foreign-official) bidders taking only 54% against a 65% average, i.e. the usual buyer base showed up in smaller size and had to be paid up to clear the issue. Fed Governor Barr's same-day "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" landed on top of that weak demand and pushed CME FedWatch's October-hike odds from 55% to 70% in a single session, which is the reaction-function logic (hawkish talk plus strong data or weak demand moves the long end) this thread has tracked all month.

scenarios.direction: The 10-year holds above 5.1% into Thursday's jobless claims and SoftBank's bond pricing, and a weak claims read or another hawkish Fed voice pushes it toward 5.2%, raising the funding cost of SoftBank's own OpenAI bond before it prices and tightening financing conditions for the wider AI-debt stack this thread and Son All-In both track.
scenarios.why: Every external-driver move this thread has logged this month has held through at least the next session rather than round-tripping intraday, and SoftBank's own tranche guidance (up to 9.875% on its longest notes) already prices in a higher-for-longer path.
scenarios.precedent: 09-16 to 09-18: the 10-year cleared 5% after the Fed hike and closed at a fresh 2007-era high on 09-18, extending rather than reversing over three sessions (Treasury's Long-End Defense 09-18 entry).

scenarios.direction: The move partly reverses by Thursday's close if claims data comes in soft or oil resumes its decline, the way this month's spikes have repeatedly given back part of a hawkish-data move within a session or two rather than holding the full jump.
scenarios.why: A single weak 5-year auction is not unprecedented and this thread has already logged several same-week reversals (09-17's oil-driven pullback from above 5% to 4.93% is the clearest instance).
scenarios.precedent: 09-17: the 10-year eased from an intraday high above 5% to a 4.93% close the same day CNBC tied an equity rebound to falling oil, on Treasury's Long-End Defense's own 09-17 entry.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 hike and the Fed's current 3.75%-4.00% target range; used here for the long-end reaction-function logic only. The auction figures (5.033% yield, 54% indirect) are BMO's read as cited by CNBC, not a direct Treasury auction-results fetch.

item_title: Investors have begun asking whether 6% is the Treasury yield that hurts stocks, Reuters reported Wednesday, with JPMorgan analysts arguing the equity "breaking threshold" may now sit in the 5.5% to 6.0% range.
mechanism: Stocks are priced against the yield on the safe alternative. With the 10-year at 5.11% and the S&P 500 near 19 times expected earnings, an earnings yield of roughly 5.3% (a back-of-envelope figure from Reuters' LSEG multiple) leaves almost no cushion over Treasuries, so each further rise in the long end forces investors to re-run valuation models. JPMorgan's counter is that the companies now driving spending and earnings (AI, healthcare, services) do not cut back when borrowing costs rise, which would push the level at which equities crack toward 5.5% to 6.0%.

scenarios.direction: The 10-year holds above 5% and keeps climbing, valuation models get re-run, and equities give back part of the year's gains.
scenarios.why: Every step of the September rate shock has come from data or supply that has not reversed (the PMI, the weak auction, Fed hike talk), and Invesco's 12-month-average test is still some way from triggering.
scenarios.precedent: Reuters cites the last time the 10-year broke 5%, before the global financial crisis, when MSCI's world index halved; on the map, the 09-16 to 09-18 selloff took the Dow down 631 points as the 10-year cleared 5% (Treasury's Long-End Defense).

scenarios.direction: Equities keep tolerating 5% yields because AI-linked spending is not rate-sensitive, and dip buyers return.
scenarios.why: The Nasdaq set consecutive record closes on 09-21 and 09-22 with the 10-year yield around 5%, which is the behaviour JPMorgan's structural argument predicts.
scenarios.precedent: 09-18 to 09-22: the Nasdaq was flat on 09-18 with the 10-year at 5.01%, then closed at a record 27,244.28 on 09-22 with the 10-year at 4.96% (AI Bear Turn).

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 hike; it is used for the long-end logic only. The earnings-yield figure is this map's arithmetic on the Reuters multiple, not a sourced number, and the Reuters piece is analysis, not a print.

item_title: Wall Street closed lower Wednesday as the 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2007: the S&P 500 fell 0.75% to 7,706.03, the Nasdaq Composite 1.13% to 26,936.04 and the Dow 352.10 points (0.68%) to 51,511.59, while Brent crude settled up 3.9% at $103.08 a barrel.
mechanism: A rising 10-year yield raises the discount rate on long-duration equities and the cost of the debt behind the AI buildout at the same moment, which is why the Nasdaq (-1.13%) and small caps (the Russell 2000, about -1.8%) fell hardest, utilities (-1.7%) sold off as bond proxies, and only energy, tied to oil, gained.

scenarios.direction: Yields hold above 5.1% through Thursday's 7-year auction and the Fed speakers, and the pullback from the Nasdaq's record extends, with AI-linked names leading the losses.
scenarios.why: Wednesday's move rested on three fresh inputs (the PMI, the weak 5-year auction, Barr's hike call) and none of them reverses by itself; Thursday's early trading extended the slide.
scenarios.precedent: 09-16 to 09-18: after the Fed's hike the Dow fell 631 points, the 10-year cleared 5% and the selloff ran three sessions (Treasury's Long-End Defense 09-18 entry).

scenarios.direction: Oil eases on US-Iran diplomacy, yields drift back below 5.1% and equities recover part of the loss.
scenarios.why: The long end has followed oil all month, and falling oil has been the input that turned hawkish-data selloffs around.
scenarios.precedent: 09-17: a rebound on lower oil pulled the 10-year from above 5% to 4.93% and lifted stocks the same day.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 hike; it is used for the long-end logic only. Levels are Wednesday closes and settles.

item_title: Meta's Muse AI agent kept driving a selloff in consumer stocks on Wednesday, with Expedia and Airbnb each down more than 7% while Meta rose 1% to lift its gain for the week to about 12%.
mechanism: Muse lets people hand shopping, travel booking and form-filling to an AI agent, so the market is repricing companies whose revenue rests on customer inertia or on being the place a purchase starts: online travel agencies, subscription products, brokers and insurers that an agent can compare on price. Firms the agent transacts through (Shopify, PayPal) and the chip suppliers behind it are bid up, so this is a relative-value repricing of intermediaries against infrastructure rather than a general AI selloff, layered on the same day's rate shock that hit Alphabet and Amazon.

scenarios.direction: The repricing spreads to more intermediary businesses (ride-hailing, delivery, insurance brokers, payments) while Muse downloads keep compounding.
scenarios.why: Reuters cites 2.8 million downloads in two weeks and average daily download growth of 55% over the first ten days; the move has already travelled from financials on Tuesday to travel and subscriptions on Wednesday, and Meta and Shopify are being paid for the same story.
scenarios.precedent: 09-22 to 09-23: the S&P 500 Financials index fell nearly 2% on Tuesday to its lowest close since July, and Expedia and Airbnb each lost more than 7% the next day (AI Bear Turn).

scenarios.direction: The losers stabilise as the disruption fears meet slower real-world adoption, and the rotation fades within days.
scenarios.why: B. Riley's Art Hogan called the fears for financial firms "far-fetched," and Truist's $28.5bn revenue estimate for Meta is a fiscal-2030 figure, so nothing yet shows customers actually switching.
scenarios.precedent: 09-23: a GuruFocus read had the financials ETF down only about 0.25% on Wednesday afternoon after Tuesday's near-2% drop, although Reuters said financials stayed under pressure (AI Bear Turn).

context_note: capital-context.yaml has no reading on consumer-AI disruption; this uses the map's ai-trade-bear-turn thread and Reuters' 09-23 close wrap and winners-and-losers piece. Weekly moves are as of Wednesday's close.

item_title: Japan's 10-year government bond yield rose as high as 3.075% in Tokyo on Thursday, the highest in 30 years, tracking the US Treasury selloff, while the yen slid to the low 158s per dollar before recovering on talk of intervention.
mechanism: Higher US yields spill into Japanese bonds, and with the yen near 158 the wide US-Japan rate gap keeps it weak, so authorities' rate checks are the only brake: a JGB yield at a 30-year high raises pressure on the carry trade and on Japanese AI-linked equities that borrow against rates.

scenarios.direction: USD/JPY presses toward 159-160, Japanese authorities intervene or escalate their warnings, and a sharp yen rally unwinds carry trades.
scenarios.why: Rate checks last week and the finance minister's warning show the threshold is being watched, and the hawkish Fed repricing widens the gap that pushes the pair toward it.
scenarios.precedent: 09-08: a yen carry unwind took USD/JPY from 156.20 to 153.93 and the Nikkei down 1,130 points in a session (The Cross-Border Rate Leg).

scenarios.direction: JGB yields keep climbing with Treasuries and hit Japanese AI-linked stocks, as SoftBank, Kioxia and Arm fell together on the last such day.
scenarios.why: The 10-year JGB is at its highest since 1996 and the transmission runs from rates into the long-duration equities that carry the AI trade.
scenarios.precedent: 08-19: the 10-year JGB pushed toward its highest yield since 1996 and took Nikkei, SoftBank, Kioxia and Arm down together (capital-context rate_regime).

context_note: Yen and JGB levels are Thursday-morning Tokyo reads from NHK and CNBC, not closes; capital-context's rate_regime notes its own BOJ leg is thin.

item_title: SoftBank priced $11.1bn of dollar and euro bonds to fund the last $10bn of its $30bn OpenAI follow-on investment: $1bn of 3.5-year notes at 8.625%, $4.5bn of 5.5-year notes at 9.25% and $4.5bn of 7.5-year notes at 9.75%, plus two €500m tranches at 7.125% and 8%.
mechanism: A BB+ issuer paid 9.75% for seven-year money to fund an unlisted-lab stake, with the base rate (10-year at 5.11%) doing much of the lifting: pricing at the low end of guidance on $20bn-plus of orders shows buyers exist at that yield, and the coupon shows what the OpenAI exposure costs to carry.

scenarios.direction: The tight pricing reopens the window for other AI borrowers, and lease-backed junk deals such as the CoreWeave-tied $1.1bn bond clear at similar yields this week.
scenarios.why: An oversubscribed $11bn high-yield deal signals depth in the buyer base that other AI-linked issuers can borrow against.
scenarios.precedent: 09-21: Meta's first junk bond, $2.3bn at 8.25%, drew about $10bn of demand (Circular Financing, 09-22 digest).

scenarios.direction: The notes slip below par in secondary trading as Treasury yields rise and AI credit stays wider than the rest of the market.
scenarios.why: Reuters reported AI-issuer spreads near 115bp against 78bp for broad investment-grade, and a rising base rate compounds that.
scenarios.precedent: 09-22: the Jane Street-leased Oklahoma bond issued near 8.9% traded at 11.3%, and Meta's Hyperion bond fell to 94.4 cents (AI Debt Gets Rated).

context_note: Coupons and dates are from SoftBank's own release; the $20bn order figure is Bloomberg's preliminary read as relayed by secondary coverage.

item_title: Treasury sold $44bn of 7-year notes on Thursday at a 5.085% high yield, up from 4.512% four weeks earlier, with a 2.42 bid-to-cover ratio and a tail of about 0.7 basis point.
mechanism: An auction's coverage, tail and indirect share measure whether end-buyers will take new supply at the prevailing yield without a concession. A near-average result a day after a weak 5-year sale says the market cleared at a small concession rather than needing a step up in yield, which limits the risk that supply alone drives the next leg, though indirect demand below its average leaves long paper dependent on yields staying near 5%.

scenarios.direction: Buyers keep absorbing supply at a modest concession, the 7-year stays in a 5.0% to 5.2% range, and the Fed's October path and oil, not auction demand, set the direction of yields.
scenarios.why: The tail was about 0.7 basis point and dealers took a normal 12.5%; strong direct bidding offset thinner indirects.
scenarios.precedent: 09-23: the 5-year sale, with a 2.21 bid-to-cover and one of the largest tails on record, was followed by the 10-year's biggest one-day jump since April 2025 (CNBC), the outcome this result avoided.

scenarios.direction: A second below-average showing at the next long-end sale would put buyer depth, not Fed odds, at the centre of the selloff.
scenarios.why: Indirect bidders took 57.2% against a 64.6% average and about 54% on Wednesday, two thin reads in two days.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 hike, so it is used for the reaction-function logic only. The 0.7 basis point tail, the averages and the C- grade are BiFu's calculation against a 5.078% when-issued yield; the accepted amounts and bidder shares come from Treasury's own FiscalData record.

item_title: Treasury's buyback of 20- to 30-year bonds on Thursday accepted $4.08bn of $10.47bn in offers, about two-thirds of the $6bn ceiling, and long yields were still higher at 3pm ET.
mechanism: A buyback swaps cash for specific older bonds, which steadies prices on those issues and improves liquidity but leaves the long end's overall supply and the Fed's rate path unchanged, so taking less than the ceiling in a rising-yield market means the programme's price effect is bounded and cannot by itself cap the 30-year.

scenarios.direction: Yields keep rising despite the operations, and Treasury enlarges or adds long-end buybacks to relieve the long end.
scenarios.why: The 30-year rose about 7 basis points on the day of an operation that Treasury filled to about 68%, and officials have already enlarged the programme once.
scenarios.precedent: 08-19: Treasury doubled the buyback ceiling to $4bn per off-the-run issue, funded by a Treasury General Account cushion of roughly $935bn to $950bn (Treasury's Long-End Defense).

scenarios.direction: The programme stays a sideshow and the 30-year is set by Fed hike odds and oil, holding near 5.4% to 5.5%.
scenarios.why: $6bn is small against the market's size, as Oxford Economics noted, and yields kept climbing after earlier operations.
scenarios.precedent: 09-10 to 09-18: a week after the 10- to 20-year operation took $5.19bn of a $6bn cap, the 10-year cleared 5% and closed at 5.01% on 09-18 (Treasury's Long-End Defense).

context_note: The offers-to-ceiling ratio (about 1.7 times) is similar to 09-10's, so the smaller fill is not evidence of fewer sellers; Treasury has not published why it accepted 12 of 35 issues. Accepted and offered amounts are from Treasury's FiscalData buybacks record; the 5.469% 30-year yield is CNBC's 3:10pm ET quote, an intraday read.

item_title: New York Fed President John Williams said Thursday it is "reasonable" to expect another rate hike by the end of the year and that the time for explicit forward guidance is over, and CME's FedWatch put the odds of an October increase at 77.5%.
mechanism: With the Fed saying explicit forward guidance is over, every data print now reprices the October meeting directly: Wednesday's PMI, weak 5-year auction and Barr's hike call moved the odds from 55% to about 70%, and Williams' "reasonable" took them as high as 77.5% (later reads were about 64% to 71%), which keeps short and long yields rising together instead of one offsetting the other.

scenarios.direction: October hike odds push toward 85% or more as claims and activity stay strong, and the 30-year holds above 5.4% into the 10-28 meeting.
scenarios.why: Williams and Barr both put a further hike in their base case, and Thursday's 197,000 claims add a firm labor reading to the hot PMI.
scenarios.precedent: 09-16 to 09-18: after the Fed's hike the 10-year cleared 5% and closed at 5.01% on 09-18, extending over three sessions (Treasury's Long-End Defense).

scenarios.direction: A softer data print or a drop in oil pulls hike odds back toward 60% and the 10-year eases below 5.1%.
scenarios.why: The long end has tracked oil as much as the Fed; with no guidance, a soft print moves odds as fast as a hot one did on Wednesday.
scenarios.precedent: 09-22: the 10-year held at 4.96% through two hawkish Fed speeches because oil fell for a fifth session.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime (asof 08-25) predates the 09-16 hike and the 3.75%-4.00% range; used for the reaction-function logic only. Odds are CME FedWatch as read by CNBC on Thursday morning; Reuters and CNBC reads later in the day were lower, about 64% to 71%.

item_title: Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export hub Yanbu had still not resumed crude tanker loadings on Thursday, two days after the East-West pipeline restarted, and a return to full capacity could take six weeks or more, Reuters reported.
mechanism: Saudi Arabia's Hormuz workaround only helps the oil market if crude actually reaches tankers at Yanbu, and a pipeline that is pumping but not loading leaves the barrels stranded while war-risk insurance at 3% of vessel value makes each Red Sea voyage cost millions, so the bypass supplies less than its nominal 4 million barrels a day and keeps a supply premium in Brent.

scenarios.direction: Loadings restart within days as Aramco builds volumes, and Brent gives back part of Thursday's supply premium.
scenarios.why: Kpler shows about six tankers scheduled to load from 09-24 to 09-27 and Aramco says it needs days to build volumes and finish pressure tests.
scenarios.precedent: 09-21: Reuters reported Saudi crude flows partially recovering as Gulf loadings increased, the last time exports improved after the 09-11 shutdown.

scenarios.direction: A further Houthi strike near Yanbu or Taif or a slower repair keeps loadings halted, and Brent tests Thursday's $108 high.
scenarios.why: Saudi forces intercepted six Houthi missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu on Thursday, and it may take six weeks or more for the line to return to full capacity.
scenarios.precedent: 09-11: drone attacks shut the pipeline and stopped loadings, and Brent jumped nearly $3 in the following sessions (Reuters, 09-15).

context_note: capital-context.yaml's conflict_risk_premium (asof 08-25) predates the 09-11 pipeline attack, so it is used for logic only. Loading status is from Reuters' industry sources and Kpler schedules, not Aramco, which did not immediately comment; insurance figures are OilPrice's summary of Reuters.

item_title: France's 10-year borrowing cost rose to a new 18-year high of about 4.7% on Thursday, more than a full percentage point above Germany's, as strategists warned the 2027 budget fight could topple the government.
mechanism: A fractured parliament, a tough 2027 budget and a rising ECB rate path raise France's risk premium: the OAT-Bund gap above 100bp, with more than half the debt held by foreign investors who may be less sticky, is being priced before the budget even reaches parliament, and the ECB is unlikely to buy bonds unless markets turn disorderly.

scenarios.direction: The OAT-Bund spread widens toward the top of ING's 100-125bp range as the draft budget goes to parliament in early October and a no-confidence vote before the 11-17 budget vote becomes plausible.
scenarios.why: Opposition to the pension freeze and spending cuts is broad, and Eurasia Group says a tough draft risks toppling the government.
scenarios.precedent: 09-18: France's premium over Germany passed 100bp for the first time since the 2012 euro crisis, up from about half that before the 2024 snap election (The Cross-Border Rate Leg 09-18 entry).

scenarios.direction: Lecornu forces the budget through with constitutional powers or a compromise, and the spread stabilises near 100bp.
scenarios.why: Pre-election caution makes a government collapse costly for every faction, and Lecornu has used the clause before.
scenarios.precedent: Lecornu did not pass the 2026 budget until February this year, using a constitutional clause that bypasses parliament (CNBC).

context_note: capital-context.yaml has no France reading; this uses the map's own cross-border-rates thread and CNBC's 09-24 read. OAT levels are Thursday intraday reads.

item_title: Oracle sent the Blue Owl-owned developer of its Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico a force majeure notice, Bloomberg reported Thursday, seeking to put off payments if the 2.45-gigawatt Stargate campus fails to come online in 2028 as planned.
mechanism: Lease-backed data-center debt is repaid from the anchor tenant's contracted payments, so a force majeure notice from that tenant, even a precautionary one, puts the cash flow behind the $18bn bank loan in doubt and hits the loan's price, which is already below 90 cents and prices how banks treat the next Stargate-scale lease.

scenarios.direction: The Project Jupiter loan slides further and lenders demand tighter terms on other lease-backed AI data-center debt.
scenarios.why: Bloomberg says the notice could alarm the roughly 20 lending banks, and the loan was already stressed before it.
scenarios.precedent: 09-18: the $18bn Project Jupiter loan stalled in syndication at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, and on 09-22 the Jane Street-leased Oklahoma bond traded at 11.3% against 8.9% at issue.

scenarios.direction: Oracle and Blue Owl both restate their commitments, the notice reads as a protective legal step, and the loan stabilises near its current price.
scenarios.why: Oracle says it is fully committed and Blue Owl says the notice does not change its financial commitments.

context_note: Bloomberg's own caveat is that it is not certain the maneuver would free Oracle from its obligations, and it says Oracle is seeking to defer payments rather than walk away as the main tenant; the loan price is one unnamed source's figure, and the developer (Blue Owl's Stack Infrastructure) is separately reported to be facing a delayed gas pipeline.

item_title: Oracle's credit default swaps hit a record high on Thursday and the yield on its 6.7% bonds due 2056 crossed 8% for the first time, Seeking Alpha reported, citing Zerohedge.
mechanism: Oracle funds a buildout that outruns its free cash flow with debt and equity, so what lenders charge to hold or insure its paper sets its cost of capital directly. A record credit default swap price and an 8% yield on a Baa2/BBB- bond mean the market is pricing some chance of a downgrade toward junk, which matters because index rules would force sales of bonds that investment-grade funds must hold, and a higher funding cost for Oracle flows into how banks and private lenders price the next Stargate-scale lease.

scenarios.direction: The credit measures keep widening and Oracle's next debt or equity raise costs visibly more, tightening terms across lender-financed AI data-center projects.
scenarios.why: The force majeure notice arrives while the $18bn Project Jupiter loan already trades below 90 cents on the dollar (Bloomberg) and Oracle told investors on 09-10 that several planned sites were not delivered in the first quarter.
scenarios.precedent: 07-20: Oracle's five-year credit default swaps reached about 2.03 percentage points, an 18-year high (Bloomberg, ICE Data Services), and this week's record is a further step on the same path.

scenarios.direction: Oracle's statements that Jupiter is on schedule and its $664bn backlog hold, and the credit measures stabilise once the notice is read as a contractual protection rather than a retreat.
scenarios.why: Oracle and Blue Owl both say the notice does not change their commitments, and Bloomberg says Oracle is not trying to walk away.

context_note: The record and the 8% yield are Zerohedge's figures as relayed by Seeking Alpha, which gave no CDS level, so treat the magnitude as unconfirmed; capital-context.yaml (asof 08-25) has no Oracle credit reading and is used for the reaction-function logic only. Prices for Oracle and Blue Owl are intraday reads from CNBC's quote feed at 3:39pm ET.
